texts.text: Abstract

texts.label: text
texts.orig: AI safety practitioners invest considerable resources in AI system evaluations, but these investments may be wasted if evaluations fail to realize their impact. This paper questions the core value proposition of evaluations: that they significantly improve our understanding of AI risks and, consequently, our ability to mitigate those risks. Evaluations may fail to improve understanding in six ways, such as risks manifesting beyond the AI system or insignificant returns from evaluations compared to real-world observations. Improved understanding may also not lead to better risk mitigation in four ways, including challenges in upholding and enforcing commitments. Evaluations could even be harmful, for example, by triggering the weaponization of dual-use capabilities or invoking high opportunity costs for AI safety. This paper concludes with considerations for improving evaluation practices and 12 recommendations for AI labs, external evaluators, regulators, and academic researchers to encourage a more strategic and impactful approach to AI risk assessment and mitigation.

texts.orig: 1. The Core Value Proposition of Evaluations
texts.text: 1. The Core Value Proposition of Evaluations

texts.label: text
texts.orig: AI safety practitioners currently invest significant talent and resources in AI evaluations, meaning technical methods to test and assess the capabilities or propensities of advanced AI systems. 1 For example, the U.S. 2 and UK 3 AI Safety Institutes include evaluations as one of their top priorities, a significant portion of AI safety technical staff within industry labs are allocated to evaluations, and Apollo Research 4 and METR, 5 which are among the largest AI safety nonprofits, both focus on evaluations.

texts.orig: 2.1 Risks Manifest Beyond the AI System
texts.text: 2.1 Risks Manifest Beyond the AI System

texts.label: text
texts.orig: AI evaluations implicitly focus on risks located within an AI system, such as the system knowing and not refusing requests for instructions on how to build a bioweapon. However, many AI risks manifest through an AI system's interactions with complex systems in the real world, making it especially hard to assess sociotechnical, 8 systemic, 9 or unknown 10 risks with evaluations.

texts.orig: 2.2 The Real World Reveals Risks
texts.text: 2.2 The Real World Reveals Risks

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Much of our understanding of AI risks comes from learning about AI's impacts in the real world. Evaluations may not significantly beat the simple baseline of incident reporting from real-world model deployments. 11 We can also learn a lot about risks by collecting information from AI labs, such as through reporting requirements, 12 or embedded government-vetted auditors, and collecting subtle, early-warning signs that external overseers can piece together across the industry.

texts.orig: 3.3 Evaluations May Not Buy Much Time
texts.text: 3.3 Evaluations May Not Buy Much Time

texts.label: text
texts.orig: If evaluations indicate an AI system is dangerous, and decision-makers decide to restrict its deployment, it is only a matter of time before AI labs can patch the particular discovered issues and undo that decision. texts.text: 4.1 Weaponization of Dual-Use Capabilities

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Dual-use capabilities such as cyber-offense, persuasion, and automated AI R&D 25 are not purely risky-they are also highly desirable for certain actors like national security organizations and AI labs. Evaluations may act as progress measures and triggers for those actors to co-opt dangerous AI systems for their own means.

texts.orig: 4.2 High Opportunity Costs
texts.text: 4.2 High Opportunity Costs

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Significant AI safety talent and resources are invested in AI evaluations, as described in Section 1. Furthermore, the current evaluation landscape is highly redundant, with many organizations building tests for the same kinds of risks on their own infrastructure. Focusing too much on evaluations may be too costly of a distraction for the AI safety field, especially if evaluations do not buy us a lot more time (3.3). 26 All these people and resources could instead be applied to advancing ML safety and AI governance, making progress on problems that actually mitigate AI risks.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: There are many reasons to suspect AI Evaluations may fail to improve our Understanding of AI risks, that the Understanding we get from evaluations may fail to improve our Mitigation of those risks, and that evaluations could even be harmful. However, evaluations do not seem entirely doomed-we just need to carefully consider how they should fit into a healthy and diverse AI safety portfolio.
